chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
title: Hostile Southern audiences and the absence of black players on tour
summary: Audiences in the South and Southwest were hostile, and black stars joined only in the north; Trummy Young stayed longest.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Of course, I also recall how hostile audiences were in certain parts of the country, just by nature of the fact that we came from New York, we came down to play for them. They would sit there, you know, impress me, show me something. They never applauded, just sat there.
All of the South, south-west. I can remember in Texas, Louisiana.
Were there any blacks on the band then?
I kind of doubt it. I don't think we took any blacks on the tours.
I think it was a very big no-no in those days, to take a black guy down below the middle of the country. It was really a big damn problem.
There were a few blacks on the Raeburn band, but you never had a black third trumpet player.

No; even the stars that we had, they weren't with us in the south; they were up with us in the north, plus the fact that they weren't regulars of the band. They would be brought in for a date, a theater date or a recording session, a week shot somewhere, but that was it, and none of them were regulars.

There was a black guy that stayed with us the longest, and even this was a northern tour, it wasn't a southern tour, it was Trummy Young. He was with us--I don't remember how long, but it was a prolonged period of time. I think at least six or more months.
The other guys, Bird, Diz, Benny Harris, Pettiford, whoever else, they were in for a few days, a weekend, but not down south.
